claims.text: At elevated temperature, the constituent phases of a multiphase eutectic HEA form protective oxide films.
The constituent phases have inherently different oxide-forming tendencies.
Oxides formed on different eutectic phases vary in adhesion, brittleness, and mechanical integrity.
Cyclic sliding preferentially fractures the more fragile oxide regions.
Breakdown of a protective oxide film exposes underlying metal and compromises corrosion protection.
Fresh metal exposed by mechanical oxide removal rapidly corrodes in the proposed high-temperature chloride-containing environment.
Repeated oxide formation, mechanical disruption, and reoxidation create a positive feedback loop that accelerates total degradation.
An AlCoCrFeNiTi-based alloy is an example of the relevant multiphase eutectic HEA.
The relevant structural mediator is a heterogeneous protective scale that forms preferentially on different eutectic phases.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion will produce higher total degradation than either isolated wear or isolated corrosion.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion will increase wear depth relative to isolated wear.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion will produce deeper corrosion attack than isolated corrosion.
Minimizing oxide disruption or stabilizing the oxide layer will decrease degradation rates.
Protective oxide or glaze layers can form on compositionally complex alloys during elevated-temperature sliding.
The proposed disruption mechanism operates specifically at 600–700 °C in aggressive chloride-containing gaseous or vapor environments.
Localized galvanic coupling between phases is a plausible alternative contributor to corrosion.
Phase-boundary embrittlement is a plausible alternative contributor to degradation.

contradictions.description: The mechanism states that cyclic wear fractures and removes the oxide, whereas the isolated-wear baseline is described as wear conducted with an intact protective oxide layer.

The isolated-wear test is required to use matching corrosive atmospheric conditions. Sliding in that same corrosive environment would itself constitute simultaneous wear–corrosion, so it is not an isolated-wear control unless corrosion is independently suppressed.
